    A Formal Calculus for Informal Equality with Binding

    Murdoch J. Gabbay Aad Mathijssen

    October 11, 2007

    Abstract

    In informal mathematical usage we often reason about equalities involving binding of object-variables. We ﬁnd ourselves writing assertions involving meta-variables and capture-avoidance constraints on where object-variables can and cannot occur free. Formalising such assertions is problematic because the standard logical frameworks cannot express capture-avoidance constraints directly.

    In this paper we make the case for extending the logic of equality with meta-variables and capture-avoidance constraints. We use nominal techniques that allow for a direct formalisation of meta-level assertions, while remaining close to informal practice. We investigate proof-theoretical properties and we provide a sound and complete semantics in nominal sets.

    1 Introduction

    Perhaps equality is the simplest possible judgement form. Informal speciﬁcation of logic and computation often involves equalities with binding and subject to conditions about freshness. For example:

    And for any binder :

    Substitution: ()[([]) if fv

    1

    1 INTRODUCTION 2

    Here fv() denotes the free variables of . It is not hard to extend this short list with many more examples.

    In the equalities above there are two levels of variable:

    and are variables of the system being axiomatised, we call these object-level variables.

    , , , , , and range over terms of that system’s syntax, we call them meta-level variables.

    These equalities are subject to freshness side-conditions fv() which make them something other than ‘just equalities’.

    A straightforward way to formalise these meta-level properties is to enrich to the logic of equality with meta-variables. In a setting with binders, we have to face the following problems:

    When is an object-variable fresh for a meta-variable? We only know this when the meta-variable is instantiated to a concrete formula or term (not mentioning meta-variables).

    What is suitable representation of -conversion of object-variables in the setting with meta-variables?

    In the presence of meta-variables, substitution of terms for object-variables becomes non-trivial: what does it mean when we try to substitute a term for a variable in a meta-variable?

    A number of diﬀerent solutions have been proposed for these problems. The state of the art solution is the higher-order approach. This uses a hierarchy of types to model the diﬀerence between object- and meta-level variables [vB01, Mei92]. An alternative solution is to reject object-variables altogether, as is done in approaches using combinators [CF58, Bar84] and cylindric algebras [HMT85, LS04].

    Unfortunately, none of these solutions allows for a natural formalisation. By this we mean a formalisation that permits a direct representation of the two-level structure which informal syntax displays in terms such as or . A consequence of this is that the formalisation of schemas of theorems and proofs are not always simple reﬁnements but sometimes requires a fair amount of emulation. In De Bruijn’s words [dB91]:

    “I think that in formalizing mathematics, and in particular in preparing mathematics for justiﬁcation, it is usually elegant as well as eﬃcient to do everything in the natural way.”

    There have been solutions to the problem of binding and meta-variables that embrace the diﬀerence between object- and meta-variables. One of these solutions uses so-called nominal techniques [GP02], which has two levels of variables, and a built-in notion of freshness of variables with respect to meta-variables.

    1 INTRODUCTION 3

    Nominal techniques have been successfully applied to uniﬁcation [UPG04], term rewriting [FG07] and ﬁrst-order logic [Pit03]. The application was purely to represent and reason about formal syntax with meta-variables.

    In this paper we explore Nominal Algebra, a novel but very natural application of nominal techniques to represent formal logic with meta-variables. In this way, and consistent with de Bruijn’s philosophy, we allow particularly natural and yet fully formal representations of the kind of reasoning which is pervasively used in informal mathematical practice.

    Nominal Algebra is a logic of equality which embraces the two-level variable structure by representing it directly in its syntax. Informal equivalences can be represented as axioms almost symbol-for-symbol. For example the equalities from the beginning of the Introduction are represented by:

    Here and are distinct atoms representing object-level variables; and are unknowns representing meta-level variables; [] is an abstraction of an atom in a term . Each equality is equipped with a freshness condition of the form # that guarantees that can only be instantiated to a term for which is fresh. The rest of this paper makes this formal.

    We also develop the proof theory of nominal algebra and show that it supports the following key features of meta-level reasoning:

    instantiation of meta-variables, by means of capturing substitution of terms for meta-variables;

    -renaming of object-variables and capture-avoiding substitution of terms for object-variables in the presence of meta-variables;

    generation of fresh object-variables inside a derivation.

    Finally, we provide a denotation in so-called nominal sets. Nominal sets were introduced by Gabbay and Pitts in [GP02].1 They have proved to be an eﬀective model for syntax with names and binding (see for example [Pit03]). In fact, nominal sets have inspired the design of nominal terms, which form the basis of nominal algebra. For this reason, nominal sets permit a natural semantic interpretation of atoms , abstractions [], and freshness #, which are not conveniently deﬁnable on ‘ordinary’ sets.

    A conference version of this material was presented [GM07b]; in this paper the presentation is revised, extended, and the proof of completeness for a semantics

    2 SYNTAX 4

    in nominal sets [GP02] is given in full detail. The authors have used nominal algebra to study capture-avoiding substitution for atoms [GM06a, GM07a], and ﬁrst-order logic [GM06b, GM07c]. Also, nominal algebra served as the basis for nominal equational logic [CP07]; also a ‘nominal algebraic’ system, but making some diﬀerent choices in presentation and design. We discuss this and other related work in the Conclusions.

    Overview We introduce the syntax of nominal algebra in Section 2. In Section 3 we provide a notion of derivation of freshness and equality with the ability to impose axioms, and we provide some examples. In Section 4 we show a number of proof-theoretical results.

    In Sections 5 to 7 we discuss the denotation in nominal sets. We give a brief overview of nominal sets in Section 5. In Section 6 we show how we can interpret freshness and equality in nominal sets, we deﬁne what constitutes a model of a theory (a signature with a set of axioms), and we show that our notion of derivability is sound with respect to the semantics. In Section 7 we show that derivability of equality (in some theory) is complete with respect to its models. We also show that derivability of freshness is not complete, but that validity of freshness can be expressed in terms of derivability of certain equalities.

    We discuss related and future work in Section 8.

    2 Syntax

    We need a syntax in which expressions with meta-variables, such as and fv(), may be represented. We use nominal terms [UPG04] because they oﬀer built-in support for meta-variables, abstraction, and freshness in a way that is close to informal practice.

    7.3 The Status of Freshness Derivations

    Deﬁnition 6.6 states that validity of freshness depends on the axioms of a theory. Derivability does not depend on axioms, it only inspects syntax. For this reason, we do not have completeness for freshnesses. That is, ∆ # does not imply # necessarily.

    For examples of incompleteness of freshness, we recall Example 7.8. We showed that in theory ATOM with one axiom , # is valid for the term model (and any valuation ). It is not hard to verify that this property holds for all models of ATOM. So we have #, but also #. Similarly, we can show that () for any model of theory LAM, so #(), but also #().

    To understand why this is desirable we must draw a distinction between the intension and the extension of a term.

    ‘#()’ has the status of ‘ fv(())’; both are false. Yet () is -convertible to and fv() holds. A freshness judgement ∆ # is an intensional judgement on concrete syntax.4 All the capture-avoidance side-conditions we know of are in accordance with the slogan ‘ away from informal practice’, this is what ∆ # models.

    Nominal sets is unusual amongst semantics in that it has an extensional semantic notion of freshness #. In fact, semantic freshness is hiding in nominal algebra in the theory of equality.

    8 Conclusions

    Nominal terms embrace the diﬀerence between the object-level and the meta-level. There are two classes of variables, atoms and unknowns . Substitution for can capture abstractions by . For instance the syntactic equality

    formally reﬂects informal practice where instantiation in of to yields . Freshness side-conditions of the form # manage the interaction between the two levels and ‘recover’ capture-avoidance where this is required.

    Nominal algebra stakes a claim to nominal terms as a logical system, and the support for binding allows us to reﬂect binding in logic directly. We have argued that this system accurately and eﬀectively represents the meta-level of equality, using unknowns and freshness conditions. We studied the proof theory of this logic and we investigated a denotational semantics in nominal sets. In this semantics, object-level variables are ﬁrst-class entities in the denotation; so an atom represents an object-level variable symbol in the syntax and in the semantics.

    From a wider perspective, this paper pursues an overall vision that names are worth talking about as mathematical entities, both in logic and in denotation. The use of nominal techniques may be a useful complement to existing methods predicated on function-spaces.

    We have seen this in the fact that we have been able to axiomatise and then study a representative sample of some of the most inﬂuential tools of computer science, including equational logic, ﬁrst-order logic and substitution. Furthermore, and perhaps most promisingly, we have seen how the ﬂavour of current mathematical systems is maintained in the nominal setting. We are particularly pleased how successfully nominal algebra captures the informal practice of mathematics, in a completely rigorous setting.

    8.1 Related Work

    8.1.1 Nominal techniques

    Nominal algebra has been used to study capture-avoiding substitution for atoms [GM06a, GM07a], and ﬁrst-order logic [GM06b, GM07c]. Other applications are ongoing.

    The derivation rules for freshness and equality (Figures 1 and 2) are inspired by the rules of freshness and -equivalence from nominal uniﬁcation [UPG04, Fig. 2 on page 480] and nominal rewriting [FG07, Deﬁnition 6 on page 926].

    Nominal algebra has similarities to nominal logic [Pit03]. An elementary but important point is that the former is an equational logic whereas the latter is a ﬁrst-order logic with equality. It is not too misleading to imagine that they stand in the same relation as ﬁrst-order logic and universal algebra — but this intuition is false for an interesting reason; see the discussion of freshness below.

    Nominal algebra was used as a basis for nominal equational logic [CP07, page 226], which makes slightly diﬀerent design decisions. Our rules (perm) and (fr) correspond to axioms (F1) and (F4) from [Pit03, page 191], and our rules (#X) and (fr) correspond to the rules (-EQUIVAR) and (ATM-ELIM) from [CP07, Fig. 5 on page 238]. Diﬀerences are:

    Nominal equational logic does not use nominal terms, and neither does nominal logic. In nominal equational logic, atoms and abstractions are modelled using families of term-formers, indexed by an inﬁnite collection of atoms. In nominal logic atoms and abstractions are modelled using the sorts of the ambient ﬁrst-order logic framework.

    The treatment of freshness # is diﬀerent. Freshness in nominal algebra is designed to model the judgement ‘ fv()’. Deciding freshness is syntax directed, always linear in the size of a term, and its validity does not depend on axioms asserting equalities between terms. Therefore # and do not imply that #. Consider for example the informal derivation

    from Subsection 3.2. Both nominal algebra and nominal equational logic represent this derivation. However, nominal equational logic also represents the following ‘incorrect’ derivation

    The side-condition fv(()) of the -equality is not satisﬁed, but in nominal equational logic freshness is ‘semantic’ rather than ‘syntactic’ (as discussed in Subsection 7.3) so we can replace equals with equals; () is equal to . Derivability of freshness in nominal equational logic is complete with respect to its semantics in nominal sets [CP07, Theorem 10.10], but it may become undecidable if equality of terms is undecidable. Derivability of freshness in nominal algebra is not complete — but nominal algebra expresses semantic freshness in a direct, though unexpected, way using equality (Theorem 7.23), so there is no loss in expressivity. In our opinion the approach to freshness taken by nominal algebra is closer to informal practice.

    In summary, nominal logic and nominal equational logic are the ﬁrst-order and equational logics arising directly from nominal sets (which, viewed as a category, can be presented as the Schanuel Topos [GP02, Mac92]). The treatment of freshness in nominal algebra makes it something a little bit diﬀerent.

    8.1.2 Higher-order techniques

    The theory of contexts [Mic01] can be used to axiomatise systems with binding. So, diﬀerently, can higher-order algebra [Mei92]. So indeed can simply-typed -calculus [Bar00]. These systems are diﬀerent and intended for diﬀerent purposes but they share a core which is in essence simply-typed -terms up to -equivalence. Just like nominal terms, this richer term-language gives more expressivity which can be used to give stronger axioms. However, meta-variables are represented by function variables, and this inherits some distinctive features from their intended functional semantics:

    You have to choose the arity of your unknown in advance. A function variable

    can be interpreted as an unknown -ary predicate — but which ? Thus these logics distribute meta-variables across many types.

    Perhaps more importantly, instantiation of these variables avoids capture. This has a side-eﬀect that it is not possible to represent a meta-variable uniformly across contexts. For example to represent a meta-variable in the context we can intuitively express as , it suﬃces to write where : ; but to represent in the context we must write ()() — must take a higher type. Since for any given we must choose a type for it, it is not possible to directly represent the context we might write as Qs, where Qs represents an unknown context (of quantiﬁers). Instantation of unknowns in nominal algebra does not avoid capture so that accurately reﬂects our intention when we write where may be instantiated in a capturing manner. Furthermore still represents in .

    Moving to higher orders engenders certain computational diﬃculties. For example uniﬁcation up to -equivalence is not decidable (although restrictions of it are in [Mil91]), while uniﬁcation up to CORE is decidable [UPG04]. Still, quotienting terms by is convenient, as exploited by theorem-provers such as Isabelle [Pau89]. It remains to be seen whether nominal algebra or something like it can enjoy the success and usefulness enjoyed by Isabelle and similar systems.

    In [GJ02, Joj04], Geuvers and Jojgov tackle the ﬁrst of the above issues by extending higher-order logic with explicit meta-variables. Although the approach of their oHOL language is similar to ours, there are a number of fundamental diﬀerences:

    The default notion of instantiation of meta-variables in oHOL is still capture-avoiding; capturing instantiation can be achieved by parameterising the meta-variable, just like in the function variable approach.

    Meta-variables are equipped with pending substitutions of object-variables in oHOL. In nominal algebra meta-variables are equipped with -renamings of object-variables. Note that we could record these substitutions by using the explicit substitutions from theory SUB.

    Besides these fundamental diﬀerences, we have not investigated how well nominal algebra can serve as a basis for implementation. From that point of view, Geuvers and Jojgov are far ahead of us.

    8.1.3 Functions

    Nominal sets provide a model of -conversion that is pretty close to informal practice. Semantic notions based on functions are models of -conversion and substitution of terms for variables. These are less close to informal practice because they do not have the ability to manipulate names of bound variables explicitly. See [GP02, Subsection 1.1] and [Pit03, Section 9] for excellent discussions on this.

    However, in addition to -conversion, we often do need substitution behaviour on nominal sets. We can do this by imposing axioms such as theory SUB from Example 2.17. If we can substitute for an atom then it has the ﬂavour of a variable ‘ranging over’ denotational elements; so SUB is a theory of ‘variables in denotation’. A detailed account of the proof-theory of SUB is in [GM07a].

    8.1.4 Binding algebras

    Sun’s binding algebras [Sun99] are based on a functional semantics for binding, whereas we work according to the relatively newer nominal semantics which is decidedly non-functional; currently the two strands are essentially independent and it remains to see what ideas might ﬂow between them.

    Fiore, Plotkin and Turi’s binding algebras [FPT99] use categories of presheaves, whereas we use nominal sets. Categories of presheaves do not have a notion of “least supporting set” like nominal sets do [GP02, Related Work]. So in its current form, the freshness judgement of # cannot be expressed in their framework. For this reason, it is not clear how an easy and direct connection can be made between the two frameworks.

    8.1.5 Other approaches

    A host of ‘cylindric’ algebraic techniques exist. These embrace meta-variables and reject object-level variables, preferring to encode their expressive power in the term-formers. Examples are lambda-abstraction algebras [Sal00] for the -calculus and cylindric algebras [BS81, ANS01] for ﬁrst-order logic. Combinators [Bar84] reject object-level variables altogether. These systems are eﬀective for their applications, but they cannot naturally represent equalities with binding and meta-variables from the simple fact that there are no object-variables.

    8.2 Future Work

    There is much possible future work.

    8.2.1 Axiomatisations of other systems

    We have seen examples of three fundamental systems axiomatised in nominal algebra: (capture-avoiding) substitution, the -calculus, and ﬁrst-order logic. In [GM06a, GM07a, GM06b, GM07c] we study the axiomatisations of substitution and ﬁrst-order logic. We would like to employ the methods of this paper to formalise reasoning on other systems with binding. We speculate on applications to axiomatising substructural logics with quantiﬁers [Res99]; also to process calculi, some of which feature complex binding side-conditions and for which algebraic reasoning principles are of interest [AG97, Lut02, KD02]; and perhaps even to logics for state such as Bunched Implications and Separation Logic [OP99, Rey02] where atoms (with suitable axioms) could represent locations and freshness might then nicely express separation. To this end an enriched freshness judgement # could be useful, generalising # and asserting a separation between the atoms not derivably fresh in and .

    Calculi of explicit substitution represent the process of substitution and so represent diﬀerent aspects of name structure explicitly depending on the particular system [Les94]. A discussion exists of how one might use nominal rewriting to express rewrite systems for -calculi with explicit substitutions [FG07, Section 9]; enriching freshness contexts with other judgements would allow reduction strategies to be expressed as part of the rewrite rules. It would also be interesting to attempt nominal algebra or nominal rewriting axiomatisations of -calculi with non-standard treatments of binding, such as Adbmal [HvO03].

    8.2.2 Semantics

    Although we have speciﬁed a sound and complete semantics for nominal algebra theories in nominal sets, we have not yet proved the HSP theorem (also known as Birkhoﬀ’s theorem) [BS81]. Freshness contexts introduce a ﬂavour of implication into nominal algebra axioms, so it is not a priori obvious that the HSP theorem survives this extension though the authors believe that it does. The HSP theorem is one of the basic results of universal algebra. It gives a valuable insight into the structure of models of algebraic theories, so this is important future work.

    8.2.3 Hierarchies of variables

    We are also interested in developing logics with hierarchies of ‘increasingly meta- ’variables. Since nominal algebra oﬀers two levels of variable, why not extend this to allow an inﬁnite hierarchy of variables, by analogy with type hierarchies in the -calculus [Bar84]? Work already started in this direction by extending nominal terms with a hierarchy of variables [Gab05, Gab07b, GL07]. We would like to extend these hierarchical nominal terms to a logic framework of equations.

    8.2.4 Implementation

    We interested in exploring how well nominal algebra could serve as the basis for an implementation of an interactive proof assistent. This may be useful because, as discussed in the Introduction, nominal algebra permits a particularly direct translation between informal mathematical practice and formal syntax; also, systems based on nominal techniques, such as nominal uniﬁcation and rewriting [UPG04, FG07], may have more favourable algorithmic properties than the current state of the art based on higher-order techniques (syntax up to -equivalence).

    A ZFA Equivariance

    We use atoms in this paper — we introduce them when we write ‘Fix a countably inﬁnite collection of atoms ’ in Deﬁnition 2.1.

    Atoms have a very special property: We can tell them apart — is true and is false — but we cannot compare them in any other way — for example there is no order . This distinguishes atoms from, say, the natural numbers, set ordinals, and so on.

    If we bear this property of atoms in mind we obtain equivariance. This is a meta-mathematical property; it refers to the assertions written in English in this paper about nominal algebra, equational logic and so on.

    Definition A.1

    The language of ZFA set theory is ﬁrst-order logic with equality with in addition:

    A binary predicate symbol called set membership.

    A constant term-former called the set of atoms.

    A ZFA EQUIVARIANCE 45

    We use standard sugar of classical logic.

    Definition A.2

    ZFA set theory has the axioms in Figure 4.

    In Figure 4, ranges over all predicates, [] denotes the predicate obtained by capture-avoiding substitution of by , and () represents any function which can be expressed in the language of ZFA sets. We also use the following sugar:

    is sugar for (() ) is sugar for ( ()) is sugar for ((()) is sugar for ( ()) () is sugar for (()) is sugar for (()) is sugar for () is sugar for (())

    The syntactic sugar used in set theory is very rich; further details can be found elsewhere [Joh87]. The only property we care about is that set theory is a foundational theory and is rich enough to express, in principle at least, all the mathematics in the rest of this paper.

    Definition A.3

    We deﬁne a permutation action on ZFA sets by:

    This deﬁnition is by -induction, a standard method in set theory [Joh87] which relies on a well-foundedness property implied by (-Induction).

    Recall that ranges over predicates of ZFA. Write () to range over predicates which mention at most as free variable symbols.

    A ZFA EQUIVARIANCE 46

    Theorem A.4 (ZFA equivariance).

    If () is a predicate of ZFA set theory then

    is always provable.

    As a corollary, () and () are interchangeable in proof and in validity on models.

    Proof

    We work by induction on the syntax of .

    By deﬁnition, implies follows directly from the fact that . The reverse implication is easy using .

    Similarly, if and only if .

    The case of is trivial, and the cases of and follow using the inductive hypothesis.

    is provable, so if and only if , and if and only if , and similarly if and only if and if and only if .

    The result follows.

    Equivariance was ﬁrst observed by Fraenkel and Mostowski and used to prove the independence of the axiom of choice from the other axioms of set theory

    [Bru96]. Atoms are atomic objects with no internal structure, so it is natural to use these to model variable symbols. This idea appears already in [Bar75]. To our knowledge the ﬁrst author’s PhD thesis [GP02] observed the application of equivariance to practical reasoning on variables in computer science as we use it in this paper.

    We have used equivariance freely in structural inductive proofs to freely rename atoms in inductive hypotheses where convenient, while remaining fully formal; this technique was ﬁrst used as part of a proof of cut-elimination for a sequent system for nominal logic [Gab06]. If we wish to be fully formal but ignore equivariance then we must work by induction on measures such as term length or derivation depth. These proofs tend to be longer, harder to read — and they are rarely given in full detail outside of a theorem-prover.
